intro: Painters can produce a sense of order by locating a figure among carefully arranged shapes or by positioning the viewer in an expansive city. The subject's scale changes what the picture seems to value.
alt: Microsoft appears amid balanced architecture, a carefully staged scene, an expansive canal view and a full-length formal portrait.

variants.name: French classicism
variants.look: Clear contours and strong architectural lines divide the scene into readable parts.
variants.history: Seventeenth-century French painters such as Nicolas Poussin drew on classical antiquity and Renaissance examples. Poussin spent much of his career in Rome.
variants.when: Study the scene when several figures or gestures need to coexist within a clearly ordered space.
variants.why: A stable framework lets viewers understand a figure's action by its position among other forms.

variants.name: Academic art
variants.look: Figures are modeled smoothly and gestures are visible from one passage of the composition to the next.
variants.history: European art academies formalized training in drawing, the human figure and historical models. Styles and institutions changed substantially across centuries and countries.
variants.when: Study a historical academy painting when you want to analyze how elaborate scenes were planned and polished.
variants.why: Shared conventions gave artists and audiences legible expectations about finish, subject and scale.

variants.name: vedute
variants.look: The view opens out along a canal, with buildings decreasing carefully in scale toward the distance.
variants.history: Vedute are detailed views. Eighteenth-century artists such as Canaletto sold recognizable Venetian views to local and traveling buyers.
variants.when: Study the relation between the viewpoint and the buildings chosen to make the city recognizable.
variants.why: Tiny foreground figures give a familiar measure against the broad architecture.

variants.name: Grand Manner portrait
variants.look: A full-length pose, a plinth and rich drapery give the sitter an imposing presence.
variants.history: Grand Manner portraiture drew on elevated classical and historical poses. Eighteenth-century British painters such as Joshua Reynolds helped define the approach.
variants.when: Study it when setting, pose and clothing must establish how the sitter wishes to appear publicly.
variants.why: The arrangement enlarges the sitter's social presence as well as their physical scale.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. As specified, she is the subject of each individual artwork's idiom, or a visitor for works that do not depict people. Style distinctions are immediately clear. Scene list in exact order: French classicism: thoughtfully geometrical composition among grand architectural forms, clear contours in an ordered idealized room; Academic art: refined studio history painting with carefully modeled forms in clearly staged gesture and smoothly finished surface; Venetian veduta: modern woman a small visitor figure in a meticulously described broad canal view and architectural perspective; Grand Manner portrait: towering full-height woman posed with one hand on a stone plinth, dark costume set against red drapery and distant estate, dignified stage lighting. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
